claim: The 14-day rule for embryo research stipulates that experiments with intact human embryos must not allow them to develop beyond 14 days or the appearance of the primitive streak.
source: The "14-day rule" for embryo research stipulates that experiments with intact human embryos must not allow them to develop beyond 14 days or the appearance of the primitive streak.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about existing research guidelines.

claim: Recent experiments showing that suitably cultured human pluripotent stem cells can self-organize and recapitulate embryonic features have highlighted difficulties with the 14-day rule.
source: However, recent experiments showing that suitably cultured human pluripotent stem cells can self-organize and recapitulate embryonic features have highlighted difficulties with the 14-day rule and led to calls for its reassessment.
evidence: This refers to recent experimental findings that have raised concerns about existing guidelines.

claim: The framework underlying the 14-day rule cannot adequately describe the ways by which synthetic human entities with embryo-like features (SHEEFs) might develop morally concerning features through altered forms of development.
source: Here we argue that these and related experiments raise more foundational issues that cannot be fixed by adjusting the 14-day rule, because the framework underlying the rule cannot adequately describe the ways by which synthetic human entities with embryo-like features (SHEEFs) might develop morally concerning features through altered forms of development.
evidence: This is the authors' central argument based on their analysis of the limitations of current guidelines.

claim: Human Embryonic Stem Cells (hESC) were first derived in 1998.
source: Since human Embryonic Stem Cells (hESC) were first derived in 1998 (Thomson et al., 1998)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Thomson et al., 1998.

claim: Human induced Pluripotent Stem Cells (hiPSC) were first derived in 2007.
source: and human induced Pluripotent Stem Cells (hiPSC) in 2007 (Takahashi et al., 2007)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Takahashi et al., 2007.

claim: Much of the effort to generate functional human tissues has been channeled into development of in vitro methods due in part to ethical concerns with and regulations on human cloning.
source: In part due to ethical concerns with and regulations on human cloning (Pattinson and Caulfield, 2004), much of this effort has been channeled into development of in vitro methods for producing these tissues.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Pattinson and Caulfield, 2004.

claim: 3D tissue culturing methods yield more complex and realistic organ models (organoids) that feature multiple cell types and patterning characteristic of mature organs.
source: Recently, 3D tissue culturing methods have been found to yield more complex and realistic organ models (organoids) that feature multiple cell types and patterning characteristic of mature organs (Lancaster and Knoblich, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Lancaster and Knoblich, 2014.

claim: Organoid development and growth are frequently stunted due to lack of effective means for delivering nutrients to and eliminating wastes from cells in the organoid interior.
source: Organoid development and growth are also frequently stunted due to lack of effective means for delivering nutrients to and eliminating wastes from cells in the organoid interior (see, e.g., Lancaster et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Lancaster et al., 2013.

claim: Neurons can be derived from hPSC in 4 days even in pluripotency-maintaining media through induced overexpression of transcription factors.
source: Because driving hPSC differentiation by induced overexpression of transcription factors can powerfully override media signals (e.g., neurons can be derived from hPSC in 4 days even in pluripotency-maintaining media; Busskamp et al., 2014)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Busskamp et al., 2014.

claim: Cells of different types can be positioned with precision using 3D tissue printing.
source: Meanwhile, cells of different types can be positioned with precision using 3D tissue printing (Homan et al., 2016)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Homan et al., 2016.

claim: Microfabrication methods can be used to create substrates that facilitate cell type development, adhesion, and tissue organization.
source: and microfabrication methods (frequently used in Organs-on-Chips approaches; Huh et al., 2012; Wang et al., 2014) can also be used to create substrates that facilitate cell type development, adhesion, and tissue organization.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Huh et al., 2012 and Wang et al., 2014.

claim: 3D printing can be used to print vasculature into 3D cell cultures and this vasculature can be connected to external perfusion apparatus.
source: 3D printing can also be used to print vasculature into 3D cell cultures and this vasculature can be connected to external perfusion apparatus (Kolesky et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Kolesky et al., 2014.

claim: The gastruloid SHEEFs generated in the Warmflash et al. (2014) experiments gave rise to a well-formed primitive streak never previously generated in vitro from hPSC.
source: Importantly, however, even the relatively simple gastruloid SHEEFs generated in the Warmflash et al. (2014) experiments via hPSC colony micropatterning gave rise not only to a well-formed embryonic feature (the PS) never previously generated in vitro from hPSC
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Warmflash et al., 2014.

claim: The primitive streak generated in the Warmflash et al. (2014) experiments had a circular shape that accommodated the shape of the micropattern and differed markedly from the linear PS of non-synthetic embryos.
source: but to a PS whose circular shape accommodated the shape of the micropattern and differed markedly from the linear PS of non-synthetic embryos.
evidence: This is based on observations from the Warmflash et al., 2014 experiments.

claim: The developmental potential harbored by hPSC can adapt readily to non-natural conditions and unfold with considerable plasticity.
source: This observation suggests that the developmental potential harbored by hPSC can adapt readily to non-natural conditions and unfold with considerable plasticity
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observation about the circular primitive streak.

claim: A key concern of the commissions that adopted the 14-day rule was to prevent the possibility of embryos experiencing pain or sentience in the context of an experiment.
source: A key concern of the commissions that adopted the 14-day rule was to prevent the possibility of embryos experiencing pain or sentience in the context of an experiment.
evidence: This is stated as historical knowledge about the reasoning behind the 14-day rule.

claim: The choice of the PS and day 14 as research limits was based on the biological understanding that neurulation proceeds in embryos immediately after the appearance of the PS.
source: The particular choice of the PS and day 14 as research limits was based on the biological understanding that neurulation proceeds in embryos immediately after the appearance of the PS, so that stopping experiments at the PS would forestall the formation of a nervous system and brain that could, with further development, be subject to these experiences.
evidence: This is stated as the biological rationale for the 14-day rule.

claim: The 1984 Warnock committee noted a wide range of opinion on the question of how long embryos used in research should be kept alive.
source: Thus, while the 1984 Warnock committee report noted "a wide range of opinion" on the question of how long embryos used in research should be kept alive
evidence: This is supported by reference to the Warnock committee report.

claim: The Warnock committee conservatively chose the primitive streak as a research limit and subtracted a few days to ensure there would be no possibility of the embryo feeling pain.
source: Noting that this still left considerable leeway regarding when the time limit should be set between the beginnings of neurulation and functional neural activity, they conservatively choose the former and "[subtracted] a few days in order that there would be no possibility of the embryo feeling pain," ultimately deciding on the PS (Warnock, 1984, section 11.20, p. 65 and section 11.22, p. 66).
evidence: This is supported by citations to specific sections of the Warnock 1984 report.

claim: The 1994 NIH Report of the Human Embryo Research Panel focused on sentience and the ability to experience pleasure and pain.
source: Similarly, the 1994 NIH Report of the Human Embryo Research Panel (hereby denoted RHERP), likewise considered many options but ultimately focused on "sentience and the ability to experience pleasure and pain" (National Institutes of Health, 1994, chap. 3, p. 47; see also p. 37)
evidence: This is supported by citations to the NIH 1994 report.

claim: There is no neural tissue whatsoever prior to the primitive streak, hence there is no possibility of any kind of sentience.
source: and again accepted the appearance of the PS as a research limit because it closely precedes neurulation, noting that "[t]here is no neural tissue whatsoever prior to the primitive streak; hence there is no possibility of any kind of sentience" (National Institutes of Health, 1994, chap. 3, p. 47).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to the NIH 1994 report.

claim: Arguments suggesting that pre-PS embryos could not yet be human individuals due to their capacity to twin and aggregate were influential in choosing the PS as a research limit.
source: as arguments suggesting that pre-PS embryos could not yet be human individuals due to their capacity to twin and aggregate were also influential (National Institutes of Health, 1994, chap. 3, p. 47).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to the NIH 1994 report.

claim: Researchers could soon find ways to generate SHEEFs that proceed through neurulation without having first gone through a PS by differentiating hPSC into cells of the three germ layers and patterning them via 3D printing.
source: For instance, through the methods described above, researchers could soon find ways to generate SHEEFs that proceed through neurulation without having first gone through a PS by differentiating hPSC into cells of the three germ layers and patterning them with appropriate signaling centers via 3D printing into a synthetic PS-less analogue of an embryonic disk.
evidence: This is a speculative prediction based on current technological capabilities.

claim: PS-less neurulating SHEEFs would be created in a condition that could be morally concerning because they could have the possibility of experiencing sentience or pain.
source: Like neurulating non-synthetic embryos, these PS-less neurulating SHEEFs would be created in a condition that could be morally concerning because they could have the possibility of experiencing sentience or pain.
evidence: This is an inference based on the biological capabilities of neurulating entities.

claim: The 14-day rule would be completely ineffective for PS-less neurulating SHEEFs because the rule's triggering condition – the appearance of a PS – would never occur.
source: But while the 14-day rule would prevent this occurrence for the non-synthetic embryo, it would be completely ineffective for the SHEEF because the rule's triggering condition – the appearance of a PS – would never occur.
evidence: This is a logical inference about the limitations of the 14-day rule for SHEEFs.

claim: Methods of generating cerebral organoids are improving rapidly and are leading to an increasing ability to model diverse brain regions.
source: First, putting aside SHEEFs that proceed through germ layer formation such as the gastruloids of Warmflash et al. (2014), methods of generating cerebral organoids are improving rapidly and are leading to an increasing ability to model diverse brain regions (Jo et al., 2016; Mason and Price, 2016)
evidence: This is supported by citations to Jo et al., 2016 and Mason and Price, 2016.

claim: Generation of nociceptors from hPSC has been demonstrated.
source: and generation of nociceptors from hPSC has also been demonstrated (Chambers et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Chambers et al., 2012.

claim: The authors conducted experiments in 2011 on Embryo Scaffold-Aided Tissue Engineering (ESATE), which involved injecting human induced pluripotent stem cells (hiPSC) into previously decellularized and fixed mouse embryos.
source: In 2011 we conducted experiments on what we called Embryo Scaffold-Aided Tissue Engineering (ESATE), which involved injecting human induced pluripotent stem cells (hiPSC) into previously decellularized and fixed mouse embryos (embryo scaffolds).
evidence: This is a direct statement about experiments conducted by the authors.

claim: The authors' hypothesis for ESATE was that signaling factors remaining in the decellularized matrix would induce the hiPSC to develop into multiple human cell types at once throughout a scaffold.
source: Our hypothesis was that signaling factors remaining in the decellularized matrix would induce the hiPSC to develop into multiple human cell types at once throughout a scaffold.
evidence: This is a statement of the authors' experimental hypothesis.

claim: The authors realized that ESATE experiments, if successful, could result in embryo-like entities if sufficient tissues developed and became functionally interconnected.
source: We originally conceived ESATE as a way of developing many cell types and tissues at once from hiPSC, but soon came to realize that these experiments, if successful, could result in embryo-like entities if sufficient tissues developed and became functionally interconnected, e.g., if brain and heart primordia emerged and the heart began to deliver nourishment to the primordial brain.
evidence: This is the authors' inference about potential outcomes of their experiments.

claim: The authors' institutional ESCRO committee found that the ESATE experiments violated no existing guidelines but asked them to keep the committee abreast of further developments.
source: After careful study, the committee ultimately found that the experiments violated no existing guidelines but asked us to keep them abreast of further developments.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the ESCRO committee's decision.

claim: The authors ended the ESATE experiments in large part due to their inability to adequately perfuse the embryo scaffolds.
source: Subsequently, we ended these experiments in large part due to our inability to adequately perfuse the embryo scaffolds, a problem that now promises to be addressable in organoids and SHEEFs through vascularization.
evidence: This is a direct statement about why the authors ended their experiments.

claim: Canonical embryogenesis acts as a central conceptual model for the entirety of current embryo and stem cell guidelines.
source: Indeed, canonical embryogenesis acts as a central conceptual model for the entirety of current embryo and stem cell guidelines
evidence: This is the authors' analysis of current guidelines.

claim: The scope of research covered by embryo research guidelines expanded with succeeding commissions as techniques and biological entities became reduced to practice and usable as tools of research.
source: The scope of research covered by the guidelines expanded with succeeding commissions as techniques and biological entities considered by their predecessors to be futuristic or in early development became reduced to practice and usable as tools of research.
evidence: This is a historical observation about the evolution of guidelines.

claim: Somatic Cell Nuclear Transfer (SCNT) had not yet been demonstrated as of the 1979 Ethics Advisory Board or the 1984 Warnock committee.
source: Thus, Somatic Cell Nuclear Transfer (SCNT), which had not yet been demonstrated as of the 1979 Ethics Advisory Board or the 1984 Warnock committee, was mentioned by both as a method under development (Walters, 1979, pp. 44ff, 51–52; Warnock, 1984, section 12.14, p.73), but was not the subject of any specific recommendations.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Walters, 1979 and Warnock, 1984.

claim: In 2005, after SCNT had been demonstrated in animals and hESC had been derived, the US National Academy of Sciences formulated guidelines for both.
source: But in 2005, after SCNT had been demonstrated in animals and hESC had been derived, the US National Academy of Sciences (NAS) formulated guidelines (National Research Council, 2005) for both.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to National Research Council, 2005.

claim: The NAS added limits for hiPSC in 2008.
source: The NAS added limits for hiPSC in 2008 (National Research Council, 2008).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to National Research Council, 2008.

claim: Parthenotes generally arrest after early divisions but can sometimes achieve the blastocyst stage.
source: For instance, parthenotes generally arrest after early divisions but can sometimes achieve the blastocyst stage (McElroy et al., 2008; Versieren et al., 2010)
evidence: This is supported by citations to McElroy et al., 2008 and Versieren et al., 2010.

claim: Since 2005, NAS guidelines have contained two separate statements of the 14-day rule, one in connection with embryo culturing and the other in connection with cells and embryos created through SCNT, parthenogenesis, and androgenesis.
source: One sign of this is that since 2005, NAS guidelines (National Research Council, 2005; National Research Council, 2008; National Research Council, 2010) have contained two separate statements of the 14-day rule, one in connection with embryo culturing (rule 1.2(c) in 2005; 1.3(c) in 2008 and 2010), and the other in connection with cells and embryos created through SCNT, parthenogenesis, and androgenesis (rule 4.5).
evidence: This is supported by citations to National Research Council guidelines from 2005, 2008, and 2010.

claim: In the ISSCR's 2016 guidelines, research limits have been organized so as to contain a single statement of the 14-day rule.
source: Notably, in the ISSCR's 2016 guidelines, research limits have been organized so as to contain a single statement of the 14-day rule (International Society for Stem Cell Research, 2016; Recommendation 2.1.3.3)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to the ISSCR 2016 guidelines.

claim: Research limits for SHEEFs should be based as directly as possible on the appearance of features or capacities that are associated with emergence of moral status.
source: Instead of tying research limits to stages of canonical embryogenesis in an attempt to preempt SHEEFs from being generated in morally concerning conditions, limits should be based as directly as possible on the appearance of features or capacities that are associated with emergence of moral status.
evidence: This is the authors' proposed solution to the problems raised by SHEEFs.

claim: A reframed research limit based on the appearance of neural substrates and functionality required for the experience of pain would be immune from the problem of bypass because it is set at the condition that directly raises moral concern.
source: Such a reframed research limit would be immune from the problem of bypass because it is set at the condition that directly raises moral concern and it would function correctly no matter whether this condition was approached via canonical or non-canonical development.
evidence: This is the authors' reasoning about why their proposed approach would be effective.

claim: The commissions that developed the 14-day rule started with a broad discussion about biological features and capacities whose emergence in canonical non-synthetic embryo development they deemed morally significant.
source: Specifically, these commissions started with a broad discussion about biological features and capacities whose emergence in canonical non-synthetic embryo development they deemed morally significant.
evidence: This is a description of the historical process used by previous commissions.

claim: The Warnock report's only mention of views other than sentience were comments about the wide range of opinion on the issue of how long embryo experiments should last.
source: Indeed, beyond its identification of the capacity to experience pain as the key moral concern for determining the length of embryo experiments, the Warnock report's only mention of other views were the above cited comments about the "wide range of opinion" on this issue (Warnock, 1984, 11.20 p. 65; see also Section 11.15, p. 62).
evidence: This is supported by citations to specific sections of the Warnock 1984 report.

claim: The 1994 RHERP committee report cites sources that recognized alternative benchmarks of neural development such as the beginning of brain activity or brain function and well-developed cognitive abilities.
source: Thus, their report cites sources that recognized alternative (and later) benchmarks of neural development than sentience, such as "the beginning of brain activity or brain function" and "well-developed cognitive abilities such as consciousness, reasoning, or the possession of self-concept" (National Institutes of Health, 1994, chap. 3, p. 37).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to the NIH 1994 report.

claim: The RHERP report cites often mentioned features such as human form, capacity for survival outside the mother's womb, and degree of relational presence.
source: It also cites "often mentioned" features of very different natures such as "human form, capacity for survival outside the mother's womb, and degree of relational presence (… to the mother herself or to others)"
evidence: This is supported by reference to the RHERP report.

claim: At least one RHERP panelist named the onset of heartbeat at day 22 as a specific event that signified increased relational presence.
source: and documents that at least one RHERP panelist named "the onset of heartbeat at day 22" as a specific event that signified increased relational presence (National Institutes of Health, 1994, chap. 3, p. 38 and p. 47).
evidence: This is supported by citations to the NIH 1994 report.

claim: The RHERP committee acknowledged two abstract capacities with a long history of discussion in the embryo ethics literature: the entry into a state of individuality associated with the loss of the ability of embryos to twin or aggregate, and the developmental potential of zygotes and early embryos.
source: On a completely different level, the RHERP committee also acknowledged two abstract capacities with a long history of discussion in the embryo ethics literature—the entry into a state of individuality associated with the loss of the ability of embryos to twin or aggregate (Diamond, 1975; Donceel, 1970; Gilbert, 2008; Montague, 2011; Munthe, 2001), and the developmental potential of zygotes and early embryos (see, e.g., Stier and Schoene-Seifert, 2013)
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to the embryo ethics literature.

claim: SHEEFs that are engineered to be very like non-synthetic embryos in features and potential will likely excite moral reactions comparable to those raised by embryos.
source: For instance, it is likely that SHEEFs that are engineered to be very like non-synthetic embryos in features and potential ("embryos in a dish" as per Pera et al., 2015) will excite moral reactions comparable to those raised by embryos
evidence: This is a prediction based on inference about moral reactions, with a citation to Pera et al., 2015.

claim: Novel combinations of features in SHEEFs, such as a SHEEF that combines a human beating heart and a brain that lacks the capacity for pain and sensation, will raise more uncertain reactions.
source: while novel combinations of features, such as a SHEEF that combines a human beating heart and a brain that lacks the capacity for pain and sensation, will raise more uncertain reactions.
evidence: This is a prediction based on speculation about moral reactions to novel entities.

claim: Some combinations of signifying features in SHEEFs could evoke 'yuck' responses that fall short of articulated moral objections.
source: It can also be expected that some combinations of signifying features could evoke "yuck" responses (Brown, 2006; Niemelä, 2011) that fall short of articulated moral objections
evidence: This is a prediction with citations to Brown, 2006 and Niemelä, 2011.

claim: A fairly detailed map of the embryonic cell types and structures that participate in cardiogenesis has been developed in mouse.
source: For instance, if a beating heart were identified as moral status signifying for SHEEFs, a fairly detailed map of the embryonic cell types and structures that participate in cardiogenesis has been developed in mouse (Brade et al., 2013) that could be integrated with embryological, cell culture, and molecular data from human.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Brade et al., 2013.

claim: Neural pathways that underlie pain perception have been mapped out at high levels, such as the pathway from nociceptors through the spinothalamic and thalamocortical tracts into the somatosensory cortex.
source: For instance, neural pathways that underlie pain perception have been mapped out at high levels, such as the pathway from nociceptors through the spinothalamic and thalamocortical tracts into the somatosensory cortex (Al-Chaer, 2012)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Al-Chaer, 2012.

claim: Uncertainties remain about the composition and functionality of pain pathways in embryos.
source: but uncertainties remain about the composition and functionality of these pathways in embryos (Lee et al., 2005; Lowery et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Lee et al., 2005 and Lowery et al., 2007.

claim: The authors propose a set of exploratory inquiries into the moral and scientific issues of SHEEFs rather than a commission for determining guidelines and research limits.
source: It is because of the novelty of SHEEFs and the many open questions regarding how to assess their moral status that we propose a set of exploratory inquiries into their moral and scientific issues rather than a commission for determining guidelines and research limits for them.
evidence: This is the authors' explicit proposal for how to proceed.

claim: The authors suggest that the research and bioethics communities lead the exploratory inquiries because they have the most immediate contact with the scientific and ethical issues being raised by SHEEFs.
source: We have suggested that the research and bioethics communities lead these inquiries because they have the most immediate contact with the scientific and ethical issues being raised by SHEEFs.
evidence: This is the authors' reasoning for who should lead the inquiries.

claim: The Warmflash et al. (2014) experiments demonstrating a SHEEF with a PS have prompted interest in the possibility of revising the 14-day rule to allow more extended experiments with non-synthetic embryos.
source: As noted earlier, the Warmflash et al. (2014) experiments demonstrating a SHEEF with a PS have prompted interest in the possibility of revising the 14-day rule to allow more extended experiments with non-synthetic embryos.
evidence: This is a statement about the impact of the Warmflash et al. experiments on discussions about the 14-day rule.

claim: Non-synthetic embryos go through the PS stage routinely and are not generally developmentally plastic in the way that SHEEFs are.
source: But non-synthetic embryos go through the PS stage routinely and are not generally developmentally plastic in this way, so this conclusion does not follow.
evidence: This is stated as biological knowledge about embryo development.

claim: The 14-day rule has been defended for embryos by reference to capacities for twinning and developmental potential, although these arguments have been challenged.
source: and also because the 14-day rule has also been defended for embryos by reference to capacities for twinning and developmental potential whose status is uncertain for SHEEFs (although these arguments have been challenged for embryos, too: see comments and citations above).
evidence: This is stated as knowledge about arguments for the 14-day rule, with reference to earlier discussion.

claim: Features whose moral significance for embryos involves relational presence would seem especially amenable to being deemed non-signifying for SHEEFs.
source: Features whose moral significance for embryos involves relational presence would seem especially amenable to being deemed non-signifying for SHEEFs (see section 4.1 above).
evidence: This is an inference about which features might not apply to SHEEFs.

claim: Realizing the promise of SHEEFs as systems for analyzing human embryogenesis will require generating SHEEFs that are as close as they can be to non-synthetic embryos without triggering the restrictions that would apply to them.
source: To realize the promise of SHEEFs as systems for analyzing human embryogenesis experimentally will require generating SHEEFs that are as close as they can be to non-synthetic embryos without triggering the restrictions that would apply to them.
evidence: This is an inference about what will be needed to use SHEEFs for research.

claim: Different definitions of 'embryo' in place in different jurisdictions today will complicate research using SHEEFs.
source: This will increase pressure for guidelines and research limits for both SHEEFs and embryos that give precise definition to how SHEEFs must be configured to avoid making them morally equivalent to embryos, aggravating the problems noted by Pera et al. (Pera et al., 2015) regarding how the different definitions of "embryo" in place in different jurisdictions today will complicate research using SHEEFs.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Pera et al., 2015.

claim: Altered nuclear transfer (ANT) involved using SCNT with nuclei engineered with mutations that would generate compromised life forms that could not develop to the PS stage.
source: Historically, this is analogous to the "altered nuclear transfer" (ANT) method (Hurlbut, 2005) put forth during the formulation of United States' policies on the derivation of hESC (President's Council on Bioethics, 2005). ANT involved using SCNT with nuclei engineered with mutations that would generate "compromised life forms" (Guenin, 2005) that could not develop to the PS stage.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Hurlbut, 2005, President's Council on Bioethics, 2005, and Guenin, 2005.

claim: ANT was never accepted into the United States' hESC guidelines.
source: ANT was never accepted into the United States' hESC guidelines, and the argument that it was ethically better than deriving hESC directly from embryos was debated (Guenin, 2005).
evidence: This is stated as historical fact with a citation to Guenin, 2005.

claim: Entities created from mixtures of human and animal cells and tissues would raise moral concerns similar to those raised by chimeras.
source: Entities created from mixtures of human and animal cells and tissues would raise moral concerns similar to those raised by chimeras
evidence: This is an inference about the ethical implications of mixed-species entities.

claim: A synthetic animal entity that presented operative and sustainedly active neural pathways for pain might excite moral concerns similar to those covered by guidelines that require minimization of pain and distress in experiments with animals.
source: For instance, a synthetic animal entity that presented operative and sustainedly active neural pathways for pain might excite moral concerns similar to those covered by guidelines that require minimization of pain and distress in experiments with animals (National Research Council, 2011).
evidence: This is an inference with a citation to National Research Council, 2011.

claim: Ethical concerns have been raised in both biological and non-biological contexts with the possibility of generating entities with consciousness and self-awareness.
source: Beyond sentience and pain, ethical concerns have been raised in both biological (Greely et al., 2007) and non-biological (Ashrafian, 2016; Coeckelbergh, 2010) contexts with the possibility of generating entities with consciousness and self-awareness
evidence: This is supported by citations to Greely et al., 2007, Ashrafian, 2016, and Coeckelbergh, 2010.

claim: Rapid advances in human stem cell and tissue engineering are leading to the ability to generate synthetic human entities that exhibit embryonic features.
source: We and others (Daley et al., 2016; Denker, 2014; Hyun et al., 2016; International Society for Stem Cell Research, 2016; Pera et al., 2015; Warmflash et al., 2014) have noted that rapid advances in human stem cell and tissue engineering are leading to the ability to generate synthetic human entities that exhibit embryonic features (here called SHEEFs) that are raising challenges to currently established ethical guidelines for embryo and stem cell research.
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to recent literature.

claim: The gastruloids generated by the Warmflash et al. experiments are the most advanced SHEEFs to date.
source: While the "gastruloids" generated by the Warmflash et al. experiments—the most advanced SHEEFs to date—have come closest to recapitulating an embryonic feature specifically covered in current guidelines, these entities are still very remote from actual embryos.
evidence: This is the authors' assessment of the current state of SHEEF development.

claim: It will soon be possible to generate SHEEFs that exhibit more and later embryonic features that more accurately represent those of embryos.
source: But given the many available methods now maturing and new ones under development, there is little doubt that it will soon be possible to generate SHEEFs that exhibit more and later embryonic features, and where these features more accurately represent those of embryos.
evidence: This is a prediction based on current technological trends.

claim: The authors sought institutional guidance from their ESCRO committee for their ESATE experiments of 2011.
source: We have already sought institutional guidance from our ESCRO committee on two occasions, once for our ESATE experiments of 2011
evidence: This is a direct statement about the authors' actions.

claim: The authors sought institutional guidance from their ESCRO committee for microfabricated hiPSC experiments similar to those of Warmflash et al.
source: and more recently for microfabricated hiPSC experiments similar to those of Warmflash et al. (which we have not described here).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the authors' actions.

claim: In both cases the authors brought to their ESCRO committee, the committee recognized the problems and was keenly interested, but could only offer limited guidance because the policies on which they relied did not cover the kinds of experiments being conducted.
source: In both cases our ESCRO committee recognized the problems and was keenly interested, but could only offer limited guidance because the policies on which they themselves relied did not cover the kinds of experiments we were conducting.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the ESCRO committee's response.

claim: The absence of a scientifically successful experiment is no barrier to productive examination of its ethics.
source: We feel strongly that this is the proper time to start this work, even though SHEEFs are still very distant from embryos, for the absence of a scientifically successful experiment is no barrier to productive examination of their ethics.
evidence: This is the authors' argument for why ethical examination should begin now.

claim: The human neuron mouse case resulted in changes to the NAS stem cell guidelines even though the experiments that led to these ethics processes had never actually been conducted.
source: A precedent for this is provided by the human neuron mouse (Greely et al., 2007), which resulted in changes to the NAS stem cell guidelines (National Research Council, 2008; National Research Council, 2010, rules 7.3-4) even though the experiments that led to these ethics processes had never actually been conducted (Greely et al., 2007; Weissman, 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Greely et al., 2007, Weissman, 2005, and National Research Council guidelines.

claim: The fundamental problems with applying current guidelines to SHEEFs lie in the conceptual and structural assumptions of current guidelines, not just in the 14-day rule itself.
source: While the ethical issues raised by SHEEFs have called attention to the 14-day rule (Denker, 2014; Hyun et al., 2016; Pera et al., 2015), we have argued here that the fundamental problems lie more deeply in the conceptual and structural assumptions of current guidelines, and that changing the 14-day rule would not address the these problems.
evidence: This is the authors' central argument, supported by citations to recent literature.

claim: Groups that oversee embryo research, such as ESCRO or EMRO committees, are well positioned to take organizing roles in the proposed exploratory inquiries.
source: We submit that groups that oversee embryo research, such as ESCRO or EMRO committees (International Society for Stem Cell Research, 2016), as well as authorities such as the Human Fertilization and Embryology Authority in Great Britain and the Embryo Research Licensing Committee in Australia, are well positioned to take organizing roles.
evidence: This is the authors' proposal with a citation to ISSCR 2016.

claim: The authors' institutional ESCRO recently organized a symposium on the ethics and future of the 14-day rule that included presentations and working group discussions of some of the proposals in this article.
